newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Army rape case jury breaks off deliberations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Army rape case jury breaks off deliberations.

text.p: Military jurors in the court-martial of an Army drill sergeant charged with raping six female trainees adjourned for the weekend after deliberating for five hours on Saturday without reaching a verdict.
The six-member jury has deliberated for 16 hours over three days after a 10-day court-martial hearing -- the first in a major sexual misconduct scandal at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground.
Deliberations were scheduled to resume on Monday.

Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, 32, is charged with 19 counts of rape, involving trainees at the proving ground's Ordnance Centre and School, and 35 other counts on charges including forcible sodomy, indecent assault and maltreatment.

Juries vote only once on each count, and a two-thirds vote by the jury is required for a conviction on any charge, as opposed to a unanimous vote in most civilian courts. Any fewer than four votes for a guilty verdict constitutes an acquittal.

Simpson has pleaded guilty to 11 counts of consensual sex and five counts of propositioning, for which he faces a total maximum sentence of 32 years in prison. He faces a life sentence if convicted of rape.
A sentencing hearing to consider punishment for the crimes Simpson has pleaded guilty to as well as any additional convictions will begin directly after the verdict.
A three-quarters vote of the jury, or five votes, is required to impose a sentence longer than 10 years.
Simpson's is the highest profile case in a major sexual misconduct investigation at the base, which has become the military's biggest sexual harassment scandal since the Navy's 1991 Tailhook affair.

Simpson is a 13-year veteran of the military, who took up his post as a drill sergeant at Aberdeen in January 1995, and has received decorations including good conduct medals and army achievement medals.
